opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think it really comes down to the nature of the workloads themselves. AI models, especially the large ones we're seeing today, simply don't fit on a single chip or even a single server anymore. Once you're dealing with models that have hundreds of billions of parameters, you need a lot of compute, a lot of memory, and very fast communication between all of those components. The rack becomes the natural boundary where you can tightly integrate all of that.

When you think about it from the customer's perspective, what they really care about is getting a certain level of performance, tokens per second, latency, cost per token, within a given power and space envelope in their data center. Data centers are planned in terms of power per rack, cooling per rack, floor space. So it makes sense for them to think in racks, because that's how they provision everything else.

There's also the matter of deployment simplicity. If you hand a customer a collection of chips or cards, they have to figure out networking, cooling, power delivery, software orchestration, all of it. That's a lot of integration work and a lot of risk. If you give them a rack that's been designed, validated, and optimized as a system, they can roll it in, plug it in, and start serving models much faster. Time to value matters enormously in this market right now.

And frankly, the industry leaders have helped shape that expectation. Once customers saw what a well-integrated rack-scale system could do, it reset how they evaluate solutions. So for companies like ours, the conversation is no longer just about how good your chip is. It's about what your system delivers at the rack level, because that's the unit the customer is actually buying, deploying, and paying to power.

r001.rationale: The response says data centers plan around power per rack and customers consider a power envelope, but it does not explain that they determine rack count by working backward from a target power capacity.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and I think the honest answer is that it wasn't really a choice customers made so much as something the workload forced on them.

If you go back five or six years, the unit of compute was the server. You bought a box, you put a couple of GPUs in it, and that was your atom. You could stack those up however you liked. But as the models got bigger, a single model stopped fitting in a single box. Now you've got a model that's sharded across eight, sixteen, sixty-four accelerators, and those accelerators are constantly talking to each other. All-reduce, all-to-all, moving activations and gradients around. The thing that determines whether your job runs well is no longer the chip, it's the fabric between the chips.

And once that's true, the server boundary becomes kind of arbitrary. What you actually care about is: how many accelerators can I put inside one high-bandwidth, low-latency domain? And the physical answer to that, with copper, with the power and cooling you can actually deliver, turns out to be roughly a rack. That's where NVLink-style scale-up domains land. That's where the power envelope lands, whether it's a hundred kilowatts or heading toward a megawatt. So the rack became the natural boundary of the scale-up domain, and everything else gets stitched together with scale-out networking.

The second piece is operational. The hyperscalers figured out a long time ago that they don't want to integrate a thousand different parts. They want to receive something that's been validated as a system. If I ship you a rack that's already been burned in, where the cables, the switches, the power shelves, the liquid cooling manifolds, the firmware, all of it has been tested together, you can roll it onto the floor and plug it in. That compresses deployment from months to weeks. When you're trying to bring a gigawatt of capacity online, that matters enormously.

And then there's the economics. A lot of the cost and a lot of the failure modes in these systems are in the interconnect and the power delivery, not in the silicon itself. If you optimize at the rack level, you can make trade-offs that you just can't make at the board level. You can decide where the optics go versus where copper goes, how you distribute power, how you handle cooling. So the vendors wanted to design at the rack level, and the customers wanted to buy at the rack level, and the physics wanted it too. When all three of those line up, you get a new unit of deployment.

The interesting question for me is whether the rack stays the unit, or whether it keeps growing. Because the pressure that pushed us from server to rack hasn't gone away. It's just going to push us from rack to row, or rack to something that looks like a small building.

r001.rationale: The response mentions rack power envelopes and gigawatt-scale capacity, but does not say customers determine rack count by working backward from a target power capacity.

astra-6.text:
Because the rack is really the unit where compute, networking, power, and cooling all come together. For an AI workload, you’re not just asking how fast one chip is. You’re asking how much useful work the whole system can do, how efficiently the chips communicate, and how much power it takes to run them.

Customers have a finite power budget and a finite amount of space in the data center. So the practical question becomes: how much AI performance can I get into that space, within that power budget? Thinking in racks gives them a way to plan capacity and scale deployments around a complete system.

r001.rationale: The response says customers plan rack capacity within a finite power budget, but it does not explain that they determine the rack count by working backward from a target power capacity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s because the problem customers are trying to solve no longer fits neatly into a single chip or a single server. You have to think about how all those processors work together, how you move data between them, and how you supply power and cooling. The rack becomes a useful unit because it brings those pieces together into a system you can deploy and scale.

And ultimately, customers care about how much useful work they can get done within their power, space, and cost constraints. Looking at the rack gives them a much more meaningful picture of that than looking at the performance of an individual chip.

r001.rationale: The response mentions power constraints, but does not say customers work backward from a target power capacity to determine how many racks to deploy.
